questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a division of labour within a shop signifies
questions.stem: While surveying workshop records, a field biologist asks what a clear division of labour between several hands usually signifies.

options.text: A shop large enough to run a programme, in which the work was planned and passed between specialists.
That the finished object was assembled by one very fast painter working alone at a single desk.
options.misconception: assumes a single hand can only produce a uniform surface

options.text: That the object was a copy, because division of labour never occurs in an original work.
options.misconception: claims division of labour always indicates a copy

options.text: That the workshop had no master, since shared tasks are only possible where supervision is absent.
options.misconception: denies a master where the records show coordination

questions.explanation: Task-sharing across a shop shows planned production with a head directing the parts. The lone-painter, copy and no-master readings each explain division of labour by removing the coordination recorded.
questions.hint: Ask what coordination between specialists implies.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey pairing picture sizes with named buyers
questions.stem: A survey of 14 market panels records the size of each and whether it was sold to a named buyer or offered without one; what does the pairing show?

options.text: Panels made for the open market cluster in repeated sizes and lack any named buyer.
Because no panel names a buyer, the survey proves that none of them was ever sold.
options.misconception: treats an unnamed buyer as proof of no sale

options.text: Named buyers appear only on the largest panels, so buyer identification is a question of scale.
options.misconception: attributes a naming pattern to size without support

options.text: The repeated sizes prove that all fourteen panels were made by a single workshop in one year.
options.misconception: infers a single workshop from repeated formats

questions.explanation: Repeated dimensions without named buyers are the signature of stock made for open sale. The never-sold, size-identification and single-workshop readings each ignore what the two columns show.
questions.hint: Compare the size column with the buyer column.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a dealer's stock of standard sizes signifies
questions.stem: A survey notes that a dealer stocks only a few standard sizes and explains what that habit signifies about the trade.

answer.exemplar: Standard formats exist because a shop must hold stock it can sell quickly, so a limited set of sizes reduces waste and lets a purchaser see at once what is available; the formats thus record the habits of a commercial trade, in which the picture was made to be exchanged rather than to be unique.

questions.explanation: Standard sizes are a commercial convenience that lets stock be produced in advance and judged at a glance. Reading them as unique artistic choices misreads what a format is.
questions.hint: Think about what a dealer needs in order to sell quickly.

questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: Calculate documentation time from the legible length of an inscription
questions.stem: A provenance check reads 38 of the 60 characters on a painted inscription, at a documented rate of 0.75 minutes per legible character; how many minutes does the check take?
questions.explanation: Thirty-eight characters at 0.75 minutes each gives 28.5 minutes of documentation. Counting all sixty characters would charge 45 minutes for characters not shown as legible.
questions.hint: Multiply legible characters by the documented rate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an ownership file that rests partly on a lost record

stimulus.body: A collection inventory records that a small oil sketch entered the collection in 1861, was sold at auction in 1904, was bought by a dealer in 1921, and was presented to the institution in 1958 by a family whose name appears in the earliest entry. A note in the file states that the 1861 entry is a copy of a record now lost.

questions.stem: Given this file, what can the survey safely establish about the sketch's history?

options.text: That the sketch can be traced back to 1861 through documented owners, though the earliest record is lost.
That the sketch must be the work the 1861 entry describes, since the copy records the same object.
options.misconception: treats a copied record as proof of the object described

options.text: That the family presenting the sketch in 1958 had owned it since 1861, as their name appears first.
options.misconception: reads a repeated name as continuous ownership

options.text: That the 1921 dealer bought the sketch new, since nothing is said about its condition at that date.
options.misconception: infers a fresh purchase from silence in the record

questions.explanation: The file gives a documented chain of owners back to 1861 while noting that the first record is a copy. The identity, continuous-ownership and new-purchase readings claim more than the entries support.
questions.hint: Note which link in the chain rests on a lost record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a destroyed work from a work that was never made
questions.stem: First decide what kind of loss a survey is recording, then choose the option that describes the consequences for the record.

options.text: A work recorded but destroyed leaves an absence that must be distinguished from a work never made.
A destroyed work counts as a loss of skill, since its makers' techniques are lost with the object.
options.misconception: treats the loss of an object as the loss of a technique

options.text: A destroyed work should be struck from the record, since only surviving objects can be studied.
options.misconception: argues for deleting documented works from the record

options.text: A destroyed work and a lost work are the same case, so no distinction is needed between them.
options.misconception: collapses two distinct kinds of absence

questions.explanation: A recorded and destroyed work leaves a documentary trace that a never-made work leaves none of. The loss-of-skill, deletion and same-case readings each erase the difference the record preserves.
questions.hint: Ask whether the record shows a work ever existed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a display does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect a display has on how a work is read
questions.stem: A survey visitor notes that a painting hung in a corridor is read differently than in a gallery; what does a display do to a work?

options.text: It sets the terms of the encounter, so what a viewer sees first and what surrounds it shape the reading.
It has no effect at all, since a picture carries a fixed meaning whatever room it is shown in.
options.misconception: denies that setting can affect a reading

options.text: It reduces the work to a decorative object, because any view without a label is without guidance.
options.misconception: assumes an unlabelled view carries no guidance

options.text: It protects the work, because a hung work cannot be studied closely by anyone at all.
options.misconception: treats a hung work as one that cannot be examined

questions.explanation: Display frames the viewing, deciding what is seen first and what competes for attention. The fixed-meaning, decorative-by-default and unreadable readings assume the encounter has no conditions.
questions.hint: Consider what a visitor meets before reaching the picture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a table of tasks assigned across many workshops
questions.stem: A survey of 30 workshop records notes, for each, which tasks were done by a master, an assistant or a specialist; what does the table establish?

options.text: A consistent division of tasks, so a finished work is a planned sequence of parts rather than one act.
That every workshop divided its work in the same way, since one method was universally adopted.
options.misconception: generalises from a table that records differences

options.text: That assistants did most of the painting, because the table records more assistant tasks than master tasks.
options.misconception: counts tasks and infers the weight of the work done

options.text: That the number of specialists shows how large the workshop's output was, since each task is one object.
options.misconception: treats a task entry as a countable object

questions.explanation: A repeated pattern of tasks across thirty shops shows planned division of labour. The universal-method, assistant-majority and task-count readings turn a table of process into a claim it cannot support.
questions.hint: Look for the pattern in the task column, not the headcount.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Explain what sale at a fair reveals about how a panel was made
questions.stem: A survey notes a small panel sold at a country fair and explains what that fact tells us about its making.

answer.exemplar: Sale at a country fair places the panel in the open market, where work was produced to be exchanged rather than to be unique, so standard sizes and reproducible decoration matter more here than invention, and the shop's output is better understood as stock answering a known demand than as a single commissioned object.

questions.explanation: Open-market sale implies production for exchange, so format and repeatability become central. A reading that treats such a panel as a one-off commission ignores the way it was sold.
questions.hint: Think about what changes when a panel is made to be sold.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the total area of a surveyed set of standard panels
questions.stem: A dealer stocks panels in three sizes of 0.20, 0.25 and 0.30 square metres; a survey counts 6, 5 and 3 panels respectively, so what is their total area?
questions.explanation: Six panels at 0.20 give 1.2, five at 0.25 give 1.25, and three at 0.30 give 0.9, totalling 3.35 square metres. Averaging the sizes would lose the weighting the counts supply.
questions.hint: Multiply each size by its count, then add the results.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: Interpret studio records and accounts as evidence of custody

stimulus.body: A studio inventory lists a chest with twenty panels described only by size, then a separate book of shop accounts naming the painters who made them and the sitters who sat for them. A later hand has added to the accounts a note that the chests were sold in the town square in a year when the town records show a fair. The survey notes that the accounts name no owner of the panels themselves.

questions.stem: Given this material, what does the survey establish about the panels?

options.text: That their makers and sitters are documented, while the panels' own ownership before the fair is not.
That the panels were owned by the painters who made them, since the accounts name the painters.
options.misconception: confuses the named maker with a documented owner

options.text: That the fair was a gift sale, since the accounts record no money changing hands anywhere.
options.misconception: reads silence about payment as evidence of gift

options.text: That the panels were made to standard size for the market, because the chests list only dimensions.
options.misconception: infers market intent from the form of the inventory

questions.explanation: The accounts document the making and the sitters, and the fair note documents the sale, but no owner is named before it. The painter-owner, gift-sale and market-intent readings supply information the material lacks.
questions.hint: Separate what the accounts name from what they do not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: State what a provenance chain is intended to establish
questions.stem: Establish what a provenance chain is meant to establish, then choose the option that describes it correctly.

options.text: A documented sequence of custody, so each holder of a work can be located and checked against others.
A list of the people who admired the work, gathered from letters and diaries of its lifetime.
options.misconception: turns a custody record into a list of admirers

options.text: A sequence of sale prices, so the rise in a work's value can be measured over the centuries.
options.misconception: assumes a price series belongs in a custody record

options.text: A ranking of the owners, from the most distinguished to the least, in order of social standing.
options.misconception: reads a chain of custody as a social ranking

questions.explanation: A provenance chain is a sequence of documented holders and events, and it exists so custody can be checked. The admirers, prices and social-ranking readings substitute a different kind of list.
questions.hint: Ask what an owner list allows a researcher to check.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: Explain what survives for study when a work is lost
questions.stem: A survey records a painting known only from an engraving and an inventory entry; what does the loss of the work itself mean?

options.text: That the work's appearance must be reconstructed from records, since the object can no longer be examined.
That the work never existed, because a lost object leaves no physical evidence of any kind.
options.misconception: denies an existence that two records independently support

options.text: That the inventory entry is the more reliable source, since written records survive longer than panels.
options.misconception: ranks record types by survival rather than by evidential weight

options.text: That the work can be safely replaced, since a reconstruction carries the same value as the original.
options.misconception: treats a copy of a work as equivalent to the work

questions.explanation: A lost work can only be studied through documents and copies, and the reconstruction is provisional. The never-existed, written-wins and replaceable readings mistake survival for value or existence.
questions.hint: Consider what a researcher can still examine.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a display does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey relating room, label and visitor dwell time
questions.stem: A survey records the room each of 25 works hangs in, the labels beside them and the average time visitors spend; what does this show?

options.text: That the setting and the label shape the visit, so the same work is read differently in different rooms.
That the longest dwell times occur where the labels are shortest, so labels reduce interest.
options.misconception: reads a correlation as a claim about labels

options.text: That works in the least visited rooms are the least valuable, since attention measures worth.
options.misconception: treats visitor attention as a measure of artistic worth

options.text: That the labels are written in a single house style, so every room reads identically.
options.misconception: assumes a uniform label style from a survey of rooms

questions.explanation: The survey ties what a visitor meets to how long they stay and what they take away. The label-length, attention-as-worth and uniform-style readings invent a cause the record does not supply.
questions.hint: Consider the effect of grouping works into rooms.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a single painted panel is often the work of several hands
questions.stem: A survey explains to a visiting class why a single painted panel is often the work of several hands.

answer.exemplar: A large panel is usually the product of a programme: a master designs the figures and supervises the result, assistants enlarge the design onto the ground, specialists handle gilding, inscription and other specialist work, and the shop's system of payment follows the task rather than the object, which is why a signed work may contain the hands of several people.

questions.explanation: Works are planned as programmes of tasks, so the hand that designed a panel is not the only hand on it. An account crediting a single maker for every surface misses the shop's structure.
questions.hint: Ask how the shop paid for the work it produced.

questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the volume of panels offered for sale in a survey period
questions.stem: A survey of 9 market sellers records 4 standard panels offered per seller per week over 6 weeks; how many panels were offered in the survey period?
questions.explanation: Each seller offered 4 panels a week for 6 weeks, which is 24 per seller, and 9 sellers at 24 gives 216 panels. Treating the week count as a month would change the total without basis.
questions.hint: Work out the total for one seller, then multiply.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a stock list showing repeated sizes and one special order

stimulus.body: A dealer's stock list records panels of three standard heights, each with two standard widths, and against each entry a number showing how many were in stock. The list also notes, beside one entry, that an example of that size was made to a client's order for a house in the next county.

questions.stem: Given this stock list, what does the survey show about the trade's formats?

options.text: That a limited set of sizes served most sales, while specific orders could still be met from the same patterns.
That every panel was unique, since the list records sizes rather than shapes of finished work.
options.misconception: treats standard sizes as evidence of unique objects

options.text: That the special order proves the whole list was built for one client, since the entry carries a note.
options.misconception: extends one annotated entry to the whole stock list

options.text: That stock numbers prove the sizes sold best, since dealers always record what they have sold.
options.misconception: reads stock levels as a record of what sold

questions.explanation: A small set of repeated dimensions with a note of one special order shows a working format system. The unique-panels, single-client and stock-numbers readings each misread a stock list.
questions.hint: Notice the note that sits beside one standard entry.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: Identify which evidence establishes custody at a dated moment
questions.stem: Decide which evidence in a file actually establishes custody, then choose the option that matches your decision.

options.text: A dated sale record or inventory entry places the work with a named holder at a known moment.
Any mention of a work in a letter proves the work was in the writer's hands at that time.
options.misconception: treats a mention as proof of physical custody

options.text: A work's presence in a collection today proves its custody before the earliest surviving record.
options.misconception: extends present custody back over undocumented years

options.text: The existence of a matching subject in two records proves that the two records concern one work.
options.misconception: confuses shared subject with a single object

questions.explanation: Custody is established by dated entries that place a work with a named holder. The mention, present-ownership and matching-subject readings propose evidence that does not fix a moment.
questions.hint: Ask whether a record fixes a name, a date and a moment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: Explain how provenance reveals how a collection was assembled
questions.stem: A survey of a collection's founding asks how provenance tells the history of how the collection was assembled.

options.text: It shows the routes by which objects entered, so the collection's character follows its collectors' choices.
It proves the collection's taste was always consistent, since good records come from good collectors.
options.misconception: infers consistent taste from the quality of documentation

options.text: It shows that the oldest objects are the best, since early pieces have had the longest history.
options.misconception: confuses an early history with a superior quality

options.text: It proves the collection was assembled by one dealer, because sequential purchases point to one hand.
options.misconception: reads a sequence of purchases as a single purchasing agent

questions.explanation: Provenance records the routes of acquisition, so the collection's history is the record of its collectors' decisions. The consistent-taste, oldest-is-best and single-dealer readings generalise beyond the evidence.
questions.hint: Follow the route each object took into the collection.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the ratio between surviving and document-only works
questions.stem: A survey lists 40 works recorded in inventories, 25 of which survive and 15 of which are recorded only in documents; what does the ratio show?

options.text: That a substantial part of the output is known only through documents, so silence in the record is not absence.
That the surviving works are the better ones, since loss usually removes the weakest examples.
options.misconception: assumes loss correlates with quality without evidence

options.text: That the fifteen lost works were the largest, since inventories list big panels first.
options.misconception: invents an ordering rule for inventories

options.text: That the documents are unreliable, since a text that records losses must also misstate survivals.
options.misconception: dismisses a whole record class on the basis of one feature

questions.explanation: Nearly two in five works in the record are known only through documents, so absence of an object does not mean absence of a work. The better-survivors, largest-lost and unreliable-text readings go beyond the survey.
questions.hint: Check what fraction of recorded works have no object.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a display does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: Explain how hanging and labelling change what visitors take from works
questions.stem: A curator explains to a survey team how the way works are hung changes what visitors take from them.

answer.exemplar: Hanging is a form of argument: a shared room groups works that reinforce one reading, a crowded corridor makes one work compete with its neighbours, and a label that names a painter before describing a picture fixes the frame of interpretation in advance, so the arrangement is part of the meaning and not merely the space around it.

questions.explanation: Display sets up the encounter and so participates in the meaning. Treating hanging as neutral decoration, or as everything, misses the specific ways grouping and labelling guide attention.
questions.hint: Ask what a visitor meets before the work itself.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of a task list assigned to each assistant
questions.stem: An inventory lists 26 panels; the master's note claims 8 for himself and the rest is divided equally among 3 assistants; how many panels does each assistant receive?
questions.explanation: The assistants share 26 minus 8, which is 18 panels, and 18 divided equally among three gives 6 apiece. The note does not list the master's other duties, so the division is what can be stated.
questions.hint: Remove the master's stated share before dividing the rest.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Compare stock purchases with a made-to-order purchase in one account

stimulus.body: A fair stall account records the purchase of twelve small panels on one afternoon by a dealer who bought at a single price each, and lists each panel only by its size and the box it was packed in. The same account shows a separate order of one larger panel made to a named sitter and paid for at a price negotiated over three visits.

questions.stem: From this stall account, what does the survey show about the two kinds of purchase?

options.text: That stock was bought ready-made at a single price, while a specific picture was negotiated and made to order.
That the dealer was dishonest, since buying twelve panels at one price is impossible in a fair trade.
options.misconception: treats a uniform price as evidence of deceit

options.text: That the twelve stock panels were all portraits, since the account mentions a sitter in the same entry.
options.misconception: carries a detail from one entry across the whole list

options.text: That the negotiated panel was cheaper, because negotiation always reduces a maker's price.
options.misconception: assumes negotiation must lower the price paid

questions.explanation: The account distinguishes ready-made stock bought at one price from a picture made to order and negotiated over time. The deceit, all-portraits and cheaper-by-negotiation readings misread the entry.
questions.hint: Compare the two entries for what they actually record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a standard market format mattered to a shop
questions.stem: Establish what a standard market format is, then choose the option that explains why such formats mattered.

options.text: A repeated size and shape that lets a shop make stock in advance and lets a buyer choose at a glance.
A size set by law, so every workshop in the trade had to observe the same measurements.
options.misconception: claims a legal rule behind a commercial convention

options.text: A size fixed by the first maker of the type, which later shops copied for the rest of time.
options.misconception: turns a commercial convention into a fixed law

options.text: A size that shows the work was intended for a church, since church pictures follow fixed dimensions.
options.misconception: assigns a religious use to a commercial convention

questions.explanation: A market format is a working convention of size and shape, adopted because it speeds production and choice. The legal, first-maker and church-dimension readings give it a compulsory rule it does not have.
questions.hint: Ask what a shop gains by repeating a size.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: Identify the record type that most securely establishes custody
questions.stem: A surveyor asks which kind of record most securely establishes that a particular work was in a particular collection.

options.text: A dated inventory or sale entry naming the work and the holder at a specific moment.
A general statement that an old and fine collection existed, without naming any of its pictures.
options.misconception: treats a vague mention as a specific record of custody

options.text: A later catalogue that groups the work with similar pictures, showing that someone once admired it.
options.misconception: reads a grouping in a later book as evidence of custody

options.text: A family tradition of long standing, which is valuable even when no written record survives.
options.misconception: accepts tradition as a substitute for a dated record

questions.explanation: A dated entry naming both the work and the holder is what places a work in a collection at a moment. The vague collection, later grouping and family tradition readings fall short of establishing custody.
questions.hint: Look for the record that fixes a name, a date and a moment.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: Compare the routes of acquisition across three collections
questions.stem: A survey of 3 collections records, for each, whether objects came by gift, purchase or bequest and how many came by each route; what does the comparison show?

options.text: That the route of acquisition differs sharply between collections, so each reflects its own circumstances.
That all three collections were built the same way, since collecting always follows one habit.
options.misconception: erases the differences the comparison was made to show

options.text: That gifts are always the largest route, since collections begin with what friends send.
options.misconception: asserts a universal ranking the numbers contradict

options.text: That bequests indicate low quality, since only weak works are left behind by a donor.
options.misconception: reads a route of acquisition as a judgement of quality

questions.explanation: The three collections acquired their objects in markedly different ways, which is what makes their histories distinguishable. The identical-habit, gifts-largest and bequest-means-poor readings override the figures.
questions.hint: Compare the three rows of the table side by side.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: Explain how fire loss sorts a record into distinct groups
questions.stem: A survey describes a fire that destroyed part of a collection and explains what the damage does to the record.

answer.exemplar: Fire loss sorts a record into three groups: works that survive, works that are recorded and can be shown to have existed, and works that neither survive nor appear in any document, and the survey's task is to keep the second group distinct from the third, since the second is a documented absence while the third is a silence that may never have held a work.

questions.explanation: Damage creates documented absences that must be kept apart from mere silence. An account that treats every gap as a lost work inflates the loss and distorts the record.
questions.hint: Ask whether the gap is documented or simply empty.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the average number of visitors held at a display case
questions.stem: A gallery survey records 9 visitors arriving per minute and an average dwell of 5 minutes at one case; how many visitors are on average in front of the case?

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a shop account that pays for separate tasks

stimulus.body: A shop account records a payment to a master for the design of a panel, a separate payment to a gilder for the gold on it, and a third to an assistant for laying the design on the ground and painting the background. The sum of the three payments matches the agreed fee for the whole panel, and the account contains no separate payment for the figures.

questions.stem: Given this account, what does the survey show about the division of labour?

options.text: That the work was paid for by task, with figures reserved to the master and the rest carried out by others.
That the master painted the whole panel himself and paid the others from his own fee.
options.misconception: recasts task payments as the master hiring assistants

options.text: That the panel is unfinished, since no payment was made for the figures at all.
options.misconception: reads an unrecorded task as an unfinished work

options.text: That the gilder was the senior partner, since his payment came second in the list.
options.misconception: reads the order of a list as a hierarchy of skill

questions.explanation: Separate payments tied to separate tasks show a programme paid for by task, and the absent figure payment fits the master keeping that part. The master-painted, unfinished and senior-partner readings misread the account.
questions.hint: Read the payments as entries for tasks.

questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish open-market production from a single commission
questions.stem: Decide whether a given picture was made for the open market or for a single patron, then choose the option that supports the decision.

options.text: The evidence of a fixed format, repeated copies and an unnamed purchaser points to open-market production.
The existence of a fine pigment and a long preparation points to open-market production in every case.
options.misconception: treats costly materials as decisive for the market

options.text: The presence of a subject drawn from a specific local event points to open-market production always.
options.misconception: uses a local subject to force a market conclusion

options.text: The survival of only one example of a repeated design points to open-market production rather than a commission.
options.misconception: reads a single survivor as proof of a market origin

questions.explanation: Repeatable formats, repeat designs and an unidentified buyer together indicate stock made for sale. The pigment, local-subject and single-survivor readings rest on a single feature that cannot decide.
questions.hint: Look for several market features appearing together.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Explain what stock made to an expected size reveals about a shop
questions.stem: A survey notes that a shop's stock included panels of a size no buyer had yet asked for; what does that show?

options.text: That the shop produced to a format it expected to sell, rather than to an order already received.
That the shop was overstocked, since a size nobody wanted can only be a mistake in buying.
options.misconception: reads a planned format as a buying error

options.text: That the panels were made for a client who changed their mind after the order was placed.
options.misconception: invents a cancelled order where no order is recorded

options.text: That the size was dictated by law, so the shop had no choice about the dimensions it used.
options.misconception: claims a legal rule where the shop chose freely

questions.explanation: Stock made to an expected format shows production answering to anticipated demand. The overstocking, cancelled-order and legal-dimension readings mistake an ordinary commercial decision.
questions.hint: Ask whether an order preceded the making.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison of documented, inferred and absent links
questions.stem: A survey compares 22 files, each listing owners in order, and records whether each link is documented, inferred or absent; what does the comparison show?

options.text: That most files are only partly documented, so gaps in a chain must be stated rather than smoothed over.
That all chains are equally secure, since every collection keeps records of the same quality.
options.misconception: claims uniform record quality across the files

options.text: That documented chains are all short, because long chains always contain later inventions.
options.misconception: implies that long chains are necessarily fabricated

options.text: That inferred links are worthless, so every gap should be treated as a break in the record.
options.misconception: dismisses a graded distinction as useless

questions.explanation: The comparison shows chains of unequal security, which is why the kind of evidence behind each link has to be stated. The equal, all-short and worthless-gap readings remove the gradation found.
questions.hint: Note how many files carry a complete documented chain.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: Explain how early provenance reveals a collector's method
questions.stem: A survey of a collector's early purchases explains how provenance reveals how a collection was built.

answer.exemplar: The provenance of the early purchases shows the collector's method rather than the collection's later reputation: objects bought at fairs in standard sizes, a few taken from a single dealer's stock, and one acquired after a public sale, so the collection began as a set of ordinary transactions which later catalogues then reshaped into a story of taste and judgement.

questions.explanation: Early provenance records ordinary transactions that later reputation flatters. An account that reads acquisitions only as evidence of discrimination ignores how collections are assembled.
questions.hint: Look at the first entries rather than the later catalogue.

questions.stem: A catalogue lists 60 lost works, and records that 2 in every 5 were destroyed in a fire; how many remain unaccounted for by the fire?
questions.explanation: Two in every five of 60 gives 24 destroyed, so 36 of the lost works are not explained by the fire. Subtracting the fire losses from the number of lost works produces the figure.
questions.hint: Work out how many losses the fire accounts for first.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a display does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a second hanging changes visitor behaviour

stimulus.body: A gallery survey compares two hangings of the same series of five paintings. In the first, the works are arranged by date in one long room with labels giving title, date and subject. In the second, they are arranged by subject in a corner with a single introductory panel and no individual labels. Visitors spent roughly the same total time in each room, but in the second room they moved between the works more often and asked for a plan of the room.

questions.stem: Given this record, what does the second hanging do to a reading?

options.text: It turns a sequential viewing into a browsing one, so the order of works no longer guides the visitor.
It makes the series more difficult, so a visitor who needs a plan has been confused by the subject order.
options.misconception: treats a changed behaviour as evidence of confusion

options.text: It proves the series is not a series, since the paintings were hung in a corner rather than a room.
options.misconception: uses a hanging arrangement to deny a series

options.text: It shows that labels are the only thing that creates a narrative, so removing them ends the reading.
options.misconception: makes labels the sole source of narrative order

questions.explanation: Removing the ordering and the labels turns a guided sequence into open browsing, and the behaviour record bears that out. The confusing, not-a-series and labels-only readings misread what changed.
questions.hint: Compare the visitor behaviour in the two rooms.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: Identify the workshop structure implied by a distribution of tasks
questions.stem: Establish which parts of a work were assigned to which hands, then choose the option that describes the workshop that produced it.

options.text: A shop organised by task, in which the master directed a programme carried out by several hands.
A single skilled painter, since the finished surface shows one consistent hand throughout.
options.misconception: reads a uniform surface as proof of one painter

options.text: A shop organised by sale, in which tasks were divided so that each panel went out at once.
options.misconception: confuses the division of work with a division of stock

options.text: An apprenticeship, in which one apprentice made the work and the master merely signed it.
options.misconception: turns a working relationship into a signing formality

questions.explanation: A distribution of tasks across named hands indicates a shop run by task, with a master directing the result. The single-painter, sale-organisation and signing-formality readings misidentify the structure.
questions.hint: Ask who directed the work, not only who finished it.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a commissioned picture from one made for open sale
questions.stem: A survey distinguishes a picture made for a named patron from one made for open sale; what is the essential difference?

options.text: The first is designed around a particular person's brief, the second around a format the market will accept.
The first is always larger, because patrons demanded bigger pictures than the market bought.
options.misconception: links a mode of sale to a fixed physical difference

options.text: The first is always by a better painter, since commissions went to the most famous hands.
options.misconception: assumes a hierarchy of makers follows a hierarchy of sales

options.text: The first never carries a religious subject, since market buyers could not afford them.
options.misconception: claims a subject rule that follows from the mode of sale

questions.explanation: Commissioned work answers to a named brief, while market work answers to a format buyers already accept. The size, reputation and subject readings attach a rule the distinction does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask what each kind of work was made to fit.

questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the group of pictures marked with numbers on their reverses
questions.stem: A survey of 40 small pictures records the height, width and whether a number was marked on the reverse; what does the marked-number group show?

options.text: That some were made as a series, since a number on the reverse indicates an intended sequence.
That the numbered pictures are the largest, because a number is only written on a broad panel.
options.misconception: asserts a size rule that the survey does not record

options.text: That every workshop marked its panels, since a marked reverse is standard workshop practice.
options.misconception: generalises a practice from a limited group

options.text: That the numbers are price marks, since a figure on the back of a picture records what it cost.
options.misconception: assigns a pricing function to a series number

questions.explanation: Numbers on the reverse appear where pictures were planned as sets, and the survey shows such a group among the forty. The largest, all-workshops and price-mark readings claim more than the marks support.
questions.hint: Ask what a number on the reverse would be used for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dated entry outweighs general praise
questions.stem: A survey explains why a single dated entry in a file can do more work than a page of general praise.

answer.exemplar: A dated entry that names the work, the holder and the place fixes the work in a chain of custody at a moment that can be checked against other records, whereas general praise establishes only that someone admired it at some time, which cannot be verified and can be repeated by later hands without adding evidence.

questions.explanation: A dated entry is checkable evidence of custody, while praise is unverifiable and may be repeated. The distinction allows a chain to be assessed rather than merely accumulated.
questions.hint: Ask what a record must fix for it to be checkable.

questions.explanation: One in four of 80 is 20 objects examined, so 60 were untouched during the year. Reading the review as touching a quarter of the years rather than of the objects confuses two counts.
questions.hint: Find how many objects were examined, then subtract.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: Establish what records combine to show a work's loss

stimulus.body: A collector's notebook records that a painting was lent to a provincial exhibition in 1911 and never returned, and that a letter of apology from the borrower followed in 1912. A separate account book of the same collector shows the painting was entered at a valuation in 1904, and the exhibition catalogue for 1911 lists it with a description matching the account book's entry.

questions.stem: Given these records, what does the survey establish about the painting?

options.text: That the work existed, was in the collection, was exhibited in 1911, and was lost in the borrowing.
That the painting was destroyed in 1911, since a loan that was never returned must have burned.
options.misconception: invents a cause of loss where only absence is recorded

options.text: That the collector was negligent, because a good collector would never lend a work away.
options.misconception: judges a practice as negligence without a standard

options.text: That the 1911 catalogue entry proves the painting is still extant in that exhibition's building.
options.misconception: treats a 1911 listing as evidence of a present location

questions.explanation: The account book, the loan note and the catalogue entry together establish existence, ownership, exhibition and subsequent loss. The fire, negligence and still-extant readings assert facts the records leave open.
questions.hint: Weigh the notebook against the account book and the catalogue.

questions.topic: What a display does to a reading
questions.learningObjective: Determine what a visitor is likely to take from a display
questions.stem: Decide what a viewer is likely to take from a display, then choose the option that best supports your conclusion.

options.text: What the grouping, the order and the labelling make easy to see, since display arranges the encounter.
Only the intrinsic quality of the work, since display has no influence on what a visitor understands.
options.misconception: denies the influence of the setting on meaning

options.text: The price of the works, since a display is chiefly an advertisement for what they cost.
options.misconception: reduces a display to commercial promotion

options.text: The names on the wall, since words are the only thing that can give a visitor a way in.
options.misconception: makes labels the only route into a display

questions.explanation: A display arranges what visitors meet and in what order, so it shapes the reading it facilitates. The intrinsic-only, commercial and words-only readings remove the visual structure doing the work.
questions.hint: Ask what the arrangement makes easy for a visitor.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret how a shop reserved passages for the master's own hand
questions.stem: A survey of a large altarpiece records that the master painted the heads and hands while a workshop executed the drapery and background; what does this show?

options.text: A division of labour in which the most valued passages were reserved for the master's own hand.
That the master was paid by the square metre, since the work was measured out before painting.
options.misconception: invents a payment basis the record does not state

options.text: That the workshop was a separate business, contracted to the master after the panel was sold.
options.misconception: constructs a business relationship no record mentions

options.text: That the drapery was painted before the figures, since backgrounds are always laid in first.
options.misconception: asserts a fixed working order that the record does not give

questions.explanation: A shop reserved the passages that carried its reputation for the master's own hand. The area-payment, separate-business and fixed-order readings import assumptions the record does not contain.
questions.hint: Ask which passages the master reserved for himself.

questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey of stock held ready for sale
questions.stem: A survey of shop inventories records for each the number of finished panels held, whether they were shown to buyers, and their dates; what does the survey show?

options.text: That shops held stock ready for sale, and the older stock was not disposed of at the first sign of a sale.
That every shop had sold everything by the year of the inventory, since stock lists are empty by habit.
options.misconception: claims a shopping custom without any evidence

options.text: That the older panels were kept because they were the best, and new work was often worse.
options.misconception: reads a stockholding habit as a quality judgment

options.text: That the dates are of painting, and not of the years in which the panels were made for sale.
options.misconception: assumes a single meaning for the date column

questions.explanation: Holders of finished, undisplayed stock across many dates show both readiness for sale and slow turnover. The always-sold, best-kept and date-meaning readings override what the record shows.
questions.hint: Look at panels that were made early and still listed.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the size of a picture reveals about the trade
questions.stem: A survey explains why the size of a picture on the open market tells us something about the trade.

answer.exemplar: The sizes carried by a shop reveal how it traded: small, repeated dimensions sold quickly to buyers choosing for a particular room, standard heights allowed frames to be made in advance, and a format that recurs across many makers usually indicates a demand the trade could plan for rather than a single commissioner's taste.

questions.explanation: A recurring size records a market expectation, not a private preference. An account that reads sizes only as individual choices misses the demand the shop was answering.
questions.hint: Ask what a shop repeats when it expects repeat buyers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Provenance and the history of a collection
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a ledger whose entries were added to over time

stimulus.body: A collection ledger records the purchase of a copper panel in 1907 from a named dealer, and 40 years later the same panel appears in a bequest to the institution. An intermediate entry, in a different hand, notes that the panel was cleaned and varnished in 1922 without recording a repaint, and a marginal note beside it in a third hand reads as found in pencil.

questions.stem: Given this ledger, what does the survey establish about the collection's history?

options.text: That the panel's route into the institution runs through purchase, later treatment and a bequest, with comment added over time.
That the panel was never cleaned, since the only cleaning entry is written in a different hand.
options.misconception: dismisses a record because of the hand that wrote it

options.text: That the pencil note is a dealer's price, since dealers write prices in pencil beside entries.
options.misconception: assigns a commercial meaning to an unattributed note

options.text: That the 1922 entry proves the panel was repainted then, since cleaning always means repainting.
options.misconception: expands a treatment record into an undocumented repaint

questions.explanation: The ledger documents a purchase, an intervening treatment and a bequest, with the annotating hands showing that the record grew over time. The never-cleaned, price-note and repaint readings misread the entries.
questions.hint: Note how many hands have added to this entry.

questions.topic: A work that no longer survives
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a documented absence from an empty gap
questions.stem: Decide whether a gap in a catalogue means a work was never made or one that has been lost; then choose the option that fits.

options.text: A documented inventory entry shows a work existed, while a gap with no record leaves the question open.
A gap in a catalogue proves the work was lost, since catalogues list every object that ever existed.
options.misconception: treats a catalogue as a complete register of all works

options.text: A documented inventory entry proves the work survives, since an entry is only made for surviving objects.
options.misconception: confuses a record of existence with a record of survival

options.text: Both cases are equally uncertain, since no catalogue can ever establish the existence of a work.
options.misconception: denies that records can establish existence at all

questions.explanation: A dated inventory entry establishes that a work existed, which is not the same as establishing that it survives. The catalogue-complete, entry-means-survives and nothing-provable readings collapse that difference.
questions.hint: Separate existence from survival when reading a gap.

options.misconception: invents a physical risk out of a curatorial decision

questions.explanation: A picture is read against what it is placed beside, so the comparison becomes part of its meaning. The fixed-meaning, critics'-company and damage readings each ignore that relational effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the pairing invites the visitor to do.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Explain why market production is easier to study than a single commission

answer.exemplar: Open-market production leaves traces that a single commission does not: repeated formats across many panels, prices that cluster in known bands, and stock held in quantity, so the habits of the trade can be read from the pattern rather than inferred from one case, while a commissioned work stands alone and needs its own documents.

That the file proves the panel was sold abroad, because a dealer mentioning it implies a sale.

options.misconception: casts doubt on a record with no evidence against it

questions.explanation: A dated bill of sale naming buyer and price is the firmest custody evidence here; the exhibition note and dealer's aside need corroboration. The other readings each overreach the file.

options.misconception: mistakes an arrangement effect for a preference for a room

options.text: That the pictures themselves are the problem, since the same works behave differently in every room.
options.misconception: blames the objects for the effect of the arrangement

questions.explanation: Identical works displayed differently produce different behaviour, which isolates the display as the cause. The best-room, room-preference and bad-pictures readings each misattribute the effect.
questions.hint: Hold the works constant and vary only the arrangement.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The workshop and division of labour
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a shop's structure can be reconstructed from partial traces
questions.stem: A survey explains to a class how a shop's internal structure can be reconstructed from what survives.

answer.exemplar: The division of labour leaves traces in payment books, in the marks left on the reverse of panels, in the pigments and grounds that a shop could buy, and in the way unfinished work passes between hands, so a researcher can reconstruct the size of a shop, the sequence of its tasks and the division of labour within it without ever finding the shop's own accounts complete.

questions.explanation: Several independent traces reveal a shop's organisation, so a reconstruction is possible from partial evidence. An account that requires complete accounts understates what survives.
questions.hint: Ask which traces a shop leaves without intending to.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Work made for the open market
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many recorded sales were resold within a fixed period
questions.stem: A survey of 64 recorded sales finds that 3 in every 8 were resold by their first buyers within 5 years; how many of the 64 sales were resold?
questions.explanation: Three in every eight of 64 gives 24 resales, since 64 divided by eight is 8 and 8 multiplied by 3 is 24. Applying the proportion to the remainder would give a different count.
questions.hint: Reduce the proportion to a simple fraction of 64.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Standard market formats
questions.learningObjective: Interpret two ledgers and a stock note as evidence of a market format

stimulus.body: A shop ledger for one year lists sales of panels at 30 and 40 units, and another for a following year lists only panels at 40 units. A note beside the second ledger records that the cheaper size had been discontinued because the frames made for it were no longer in stock. Two surviving panels in a private collection are 30 units tall.

questions.stem: From this ledger and the two survivors, what does the survey establish?

options.text: That the 30-unit size was a standard shop format with a real market, which later disappeared from the shop's stock.
That the 30-unit panels in the private collection were made by the same shop, since the size matches.
options.misconception: treats a matching size as a link to a particular workshop

options.text: That frames, not pictures, set the sizes, so the format was decided by joiners rather than shops.
options.misconception: moves the decision about size to a trade outside the record

options.text: That the 30-unit format was always a loss-making line, since the shop stopped selling it.
options.misconception: infers losses from a change of stock

questions.explanation: Two ledgers and a stock note show a market format that the shop then dropped, while the surviving examples prove the size continued in use elsewhere. The same-shop, frames-decide and loss-making readings overreach.
questions.hint: Read the ledgers with the note before turning to the collection.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What establishes provenance
questions.learningObjective: State exactly what a dated provenance document proves
questions.stem: Establish whether a document proves custody, and then choose the option that states what the document does prove.

options.text: A dated entry naming the work and its holder fixes custody at that moment, and nothing beyond it.
A dated entry fixes custody for the whole of the period before it, since the holder had the work earlier.
options.misconception: extends a moment's custody backwards over unknown years

options.text: A dated entry fixes the work's appearance as well, since the entry describes what was sold.
options.misconception: assumes every entry includes a description of appearance

options.text: A dated entry proves the holder was the work's first owner, since entries begin with the first purchase.
options.misconception: assumes entries begin at the first purchase in every case

questions.explanation: A dated entry fixes one moment of custody, no more. The earlier-period, appearance and first-owner readings each claim reach the entry does not have.
questions.hint: Hold a record to the moment it actually fixes.
